To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Lore-2 region of the mouse genome specifies the sensitivity of the locomotor response to ethanol and that the Lore-3 region specifies sensitivity of the sedative/hypontic response to ethanol.

1) the Lore-1 gene region is associated with sensitivity to ethanol-induced activation in humans, 2) the Lore-3 gene region is associated to sedative/hynoptic effects of ethanol and 3) the Lore-2 gene region is associated both to ethanol-induced activation and to sedative/hypoctic effects of ethanol.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genes that contribute to the sensitivity of the mouse to ethanol.

the identification and characterization of genetic factors that contribute to the sensitivity of ethanol-induced behaviors, and with the identification of the neurobiological substrates of these genetic factors.
a genetic region on rat chromosome 1 that is involved in sensitivity to ethanol and other sedative-hypnotics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

ethanol-induced activation is a genetically complex trait, with multiple loci and environmental factors contributing to its expression, but that a major locus is present on mouse chromosome 1, in the region between 40 and 50 cM, with a second major locus on chromosome 4, in the region of 40 cM.
the Lore-2 region of the genome is responsible for the activation of ethanol-induced behavior.

the Lore-2 locus specifies ethanol sensitivity in the absence of ethanol-induced activation and that the Lore-3 locus specifies ethanol sensitivity with ethanol-induced activation, whereas the Lore-1 locus specifies ethanol-induced activation independent of ethanol sensitivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a genetic region that specifies the sensitivity to ethanol-induced sedation and that this region also specifies sensitivity to ethanol-induced activation.
we have found that the Lore-3 region of the mouse genome specifies ethanol-induced activation.
the Lore-2 and Lore-1 regions are necessary and sufficient to mediate sedative/hypnogenic and ethanol-induced activation responses, respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Lore- 1 region is a major site of action of ethanol in the brain and that this region is involved in both sedative/hyp-notic and stimulant actions of ethanol in addition to other actions such as the activation of locomotor activity.
we can now use a single gene to predict the behavioral effects of alcohol in mice, and we are working on a test to predict alcohol effects in humans
there is no evidence that the Lore-2 region is responsible for ethanol's effects on the brain.
